newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM to meet with villagers over protest.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM to meet with villagers over protest.

text.p: Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said on Sunday he would hold talks with thousands of poor villagers who have descended on the capital to demand economic relief.

The well-organised group of about 7,000 people from Thailand's northeast, members of the so-called Assembly of the Poor social movement, poured into the capital in buses, trucks and trains beginning late on Friday.
Equipped with food and gear for cooking and camping, the villagers vowed to stay outside the main government offices until their problems were resolved.
The government made mobile toilets and medical assistance available to the demonstrators, and put police on stand-by.

The villaggers called for government help in shoring up low prices of their main crop, tapioca, which have hit them hard. They also demanded an end to the loss of farmland to government projects and a waiver of debts owed to the state-run Agriculture and Cooperatives Bank.

"I will hold talks with them tomorrow on how to raise prices of tapioca, and at the same time I would like to appeal to those elderly people taking part in the rally to give the government time to resolve their problems," Chavalit told reporters.

Bamrung Kayota, secretary-general of the Assembly of the Poor, which organised the demonstration, said he welcomed the government's quick response but was pessimistic that much would be done about the villagers' problems.
"The price of tapioca is one among dozens of problems. The government cannot bring up just one issue and ignore the others. We want a package discussion," the political activist said.
The group has made several similar protests in recent years that have almost always ended with the government promising to set up committees to study its demands.

"This time the protest will not merely end with the setting up of committees, but the government has to issue a written agreement that they will look into all our demands. Otherwise we continue to stay here, no matter weeks or months," Bamrung said.
The villagers' presence around Government House irritated some officials.
"This is not right, for everyone to come to Bangkok and camp here and demand what they want," said Chingchai Mongkontham, a minister attached to the Prime Minister's office.
He said government could only try to solve the tapioca price problem.

"The problems of land disputes and debt are not easy tasks. Especially on the debt, those who borrowed money from the bank should have known that they would have to repay the debt by themselves and not that the state would repay their debt for them," the minister said.
